## Simulation methods

### Simulation model

We make use of the simulation model of toad spread developed by Tingley et al., and updated by Southwell et al., and Dunlop et al. The model is described in these previous papers, so we describe it here only briefly. The model describes spread across a 2-dimensional landscape of waterpoints, where the probability of an individual moving between points is given by a truncated continuous 2-dimensional dispersal kernel, $t_n(u_n, v_n, \hat d_n)$: a 2-dimensional t-distribution, with shape and scale parameters $u$ and $v$ respectively, and a truncation distance of $\hat d_n$.

The dispersal kernel parameters around each waterpoint, $i$, are determined by the mean number of rainy days (rainfall \>1mm) at that waterpoint over the last 20 years. As per Tingley et al, we assume that each day of rain equates to three days of movement, and we calculate the number of days of movement at a waterpoint, $n_i$, according to a simple union of probabilities to ensure that $n_i \leq 365$. To estimate $u_n$ and $v_n$, we use paths of radiotelemtered free-ranging toads sampled during the wet seasons from the (then) invasion front east of Darwin in 2006-8 (Brown et al.). For each telemetered individual path, we resampled movement distances and turning angles over $n$ days to generate a simulated dispersal distance, $d^*_n$. For each of the XX radiotelemetered toads in the dataset, we resampled $d^*$ 10,000 times, preserving individual variation in dispersal and generating a total of XX values of $d^*_n$ for each value of $n$. These are our simulated dispersal distributions to which we fit the n-wise kernel. We also use these simulated distributions to determine the truncation distance, $\hat d_n$ as $1.1 \times$ the maximum simulated dispersal distance at each given $n$.

The dispersal kernel around each point is converted to a population density by multiplying by the number of propagules emerging from each point, $\lambda_i$. The expected number of individuals arriving at uncolonised points is then the sum of densities accruing to that point from all colonised points. This sum is multiplied by $\pi r^2$, where $r$ is the detection radius around each waterpoint, to give an expected number of colonists. The realised number of colonists, $c_i$, arriving is then the outcome of a draw from a multinomial distribution (Tingley et al.). Points where the realised number of colonists is $c_i \geq 2$ are then considered colonised and will emit $\lambda_i$ colonists in the next time step.

Tingley et al. fit this model to the spread of toads in Australia's Victoria River District using a rejection ABC algorithm and show that the invasion speed of this model is determined by $r$ and $\lambda$, but that these two parameters are essentially non-identifiable: the same speed can be given by a large $\lambda$ and small $r$ or vice versa. Here, we take a pragmatic approach to this and simply set $r = 300$m and estimate a value of $\lambda$ given this value of $r$. Our interest is in a model that recapitulates observed invasion history, not in estimating true biological values for these parameters. Choosing $r = 300$ is a pragmatic choice here because it minimises overlap between areas of attraction around each waterpoint, avoiding the need for complex numerical corrections for overlap in the model.

Given cane toads have now invaded the entire Kimberley since the Tingley model was first fit, we re-fit the model to the observed spread of cane toads through the Kimberley region. This process was described in Dunlop et al. (supp. material), and provides us with a much sharper estimate of $\lambda$ than was available previously.

### Estimating the timing of toad arrival at the TCZ

For this question we used maps of permanent waterpoints derived from Geosciences Australia's XX and YY **step out details, as per Dunlop et al**. This dataset was supplemented by manually digitising unmarked pastoral and other human-made water points from aerial imagery (Google Earth) between the toads' invasion front in 2025 across the Dampier peninsula and down to the TCZ.

To initialise the spread model for this question, we used data on the location of the toad invasion as of August 2025 as a baseline from which to forecast arrival time. The location and orientation of the invasion front in this year was very well resolved by a large set of nocturnal visual surveys across the invasion front (Phillips, Dempster, et al). Detection probabilities are high at this time of year and so there is little uncertainty as to the estimation of the location and orientation of the front. The northern and southern edges of the invasion were less well resolved, however. To set the northern edge, we assumed that toads would need to negotiate around the mouth of the Fitzroy River (-17.633614, 123.444807) and their northward spread from this landscape bottleneck was at the same rate as their westward spread. This assumption set our northern limit. The southern limit was chosen primarily on the presence of permanent water, here we chose a southern limit by eye, at a latitude of -18.514959 degrees. Points to the north of this and to the east of the invasion front were considered colonised (see @fig-time-to-tcz).

![Permanent waterpoints in north-western Australia across which the spread model was run. The red dashed line shows the orientation and westward extent of the toad invasion as of August 2025. Points in blue were initialised as colonised at the beginning of model runs that were aimed at estimating the date of arrival at the top of the TCZ (shown in the red polygon).](../out/time-to-tcz.pdf){#fig-time-to-tcz}

Following initialisation we ran 100 replicates of the invasion model, stopping the model when at least one of the points inside the TCZ area was colonised. This process yielded a sample of 100 simulated arrival times.

### Optimising the design of the TCZ

#### Auditing artificial waterpoints

In May-June of 2026, we undertook a comprehensive audit of all artificial watersources inside the TCZ management area. For each agricultural holding, we worked with the station manager to drive around the property and log every water source. This work also involved, for each water source, identifying best options for repair/replacement/upgrade or fencing of each water source.

We then repeated this exercise with representatives of Indigenous landholder groups (Karajarri, Nyangumarta). This second pass allowed us to catalogue infrastructure managed by these groups (outstations, and the community of Bidyedanga), and also to provide oversight to Indigenous landowners of the planned infrastructure works around pastoral infrastructure. This oversight allowed Indigenous landowners to visit rarely visited parts of their country, to identify any risks to cultural heritage, and to pause or halt any intended work if risks were identified.

This exercise gave a us a comprehensive overview of the work required to toad-proof each piece of infrastructure (and so a price for each piece of infrastructure), and also to identify any areas that may be difficult or impossible to manage for cultural reasons.

#### Auditing natural waterpoints

Natural waterpoints in this area are highly dynamic. Water is widespread during the wet season, with many temporary pools and soaks. By the end of the dry season, however, relatively few natural waterpoints remain. It is these permanent points that will be critical for toad survival and which we seek to map. We initially used geosciences Australia mapping to identify these permanent waterpoints (Tingley, Southwell), but site visits and discussions with local stakeholders since this initial work showed that many of these mapped permanent waterpoints were incorrect. Often perennial water was identified as permanent, occasionally salt water was identified as fresh, and occasionally points were simply in the wrong place.

Although the Geosciences Australia data is probably sufficient for broad scale modelling (which really just requires local density of waterpoints, with precise location being less important), to design the TCZ really requires accurate localisation of each waterpoints. Because of the aforementioned issues, we took the path of local knowledge over remote sensing. We take the view that the area's Traditional Owners, more than anyone else, will know where permanent water will be in this landscape. To this end we made use of an Anthropolgical report, *Ngapa Kunangkul: Living Water*, (Yu, 1999) examining the cultural significance of groundwater to Karajarri and other Traditional Owners (TOs henceforth) in the areas over which the TCZ looks to be situated. As well as detailing TOs' concerns over groundwater extraction, the report maps culturally significant waterpoints, including permanent water, springs (perennial and non-perrenial) and soaks (perennial only). To locate permanent water, springs and (non-perennial) soaks, we georectified the map provided in the Living Waters report (Map 2), and then digitised points, cross referencing with aerial imagery (from Google Earth) to generate precise locations. This resulted in 33 waterpoints (permanent waterpoints + springs), and XX soaks being identified within and to the east of the proposed TCZ area.

We treated springs as places that will dry with some probability in any given year. This reflects the reality on the ground, where the depth of the water table fluctuates seasonally, and where some of the springs have not been opened by Indigenous custodians for many years and so are no longer apparent on the surface. To understand drying probability we took two complementary approaches. First, we cross-referenced spring locations against waterpoints identified by the Digital Earth Australia (DEA) dataset (**REF**), which makes use of landsat images over Australia, with satellite passes every 16 days since 1985. These satellite images have been processed to identify waterpoints and measure their percentage fullness at each clear (*i.e.*, not affected by cloud cover) pass of the satellite. We then spatially joined the living waters set to the DEA dataset. With the constraint that the living waters point needed to be within 100m of the DEA polygon, we generated XX matches. This gives us a set of springs that produce waterbodies large enough to be visually observed. For this set, we used the DEA data to score whether or not the spring dried out (*i.e.* reached 0% wetness) in the dry season (June-December) each year. For each of these points, we then extracted the rainfall falling in the previous wet season (Dec-May) of each scored year from the SILO database (**REF**). We then fitted a predictor function for the probability of drying as a function of the precipitation total of the previous wet season plus the effect of the wet season before that, with a random effect for site.

For all natural waterpoints, including those with and without DEA matches, we elicited Traditional Owner knowledge of dry-season water persistence using a structured, map-based survey. The survey was undertaken only after consent was obtained through appropriate channels, and individual participation was voluntary. For each waterpoint, participants were asked whether the place dried out before the following wet season: never, some years, most years, or every year. Participants were also asked how the waterpoint behaved after large, average and poor wet seasons, and after two poor wet seasons in succession. Responses were recorded only where participants agreed that the information could be used for modelling; culturally restricted information was not recorded or was excluded from the analytical dataset according to participant direction.

We calibrated the qualitative drying categories using waterpoints for which both DEA-derived drying histories and Traditional Owner assessments were available. Annual DEA drying outcomes were modelled as Bernoulli trials with drying probability depending on rainfall in the preceding wet season and the wet season before that, with a waterpoint-level random effect. The long-run drying probability implied by this model was then related to Traditional Owner category scores using an ordered logistic observation model. For waterpoints without DEA matches, category scores were used to infer the waterpoint-level drying probability, allowing annual drying probabilities to be predicted for any rainfall history while propagating uncertainty in both the rainfall response and the qualitative calibration.

#### Modelled scenario

We modelled the zone's ability to stall the toad invasion over a 50-year time horizon. One of the key concerns raised by broader stakeholders is "what about extremely wet years, will the zone still hold in an extreme year?" This concern was addressed initially by Southwell et al. who modeled the possibility that in wet years toads would have more opportunity to move. This made little difference to the strength of waterless barriers in their tested scenarios. Here, we instead explore the possibility that, in extreme wet years, some of the normally perennial waterpoints might not dry up and so become a source of propagules in the following year. To do this, we used rainfall data from the last 27 years as a reference set, and used our predictor function (above) to predict the drying probability for each waterpoint in each of the previous 25 years, yielding a year by waterpoint matrix. To generate a 50-year time series, we simply repeated the rows of this matrix of drying probabilities. For a given model run, whether or not a waterbody remains wet over a dry season was taken as a draw from a Bernoulli distribution under the complement of the predicted drying probability.

For extremely wet years (defined here as the top 20% of wet years) we also allowed toads to move further, by assuming that the number of rainy days available to them was equal to the number of rainy days seen in the year with the highest number of rainy days in the last 25 years. This latter assumption yielded an 'extreme dispersal kernel'. Thus, for any given modelled year, the model would chose from either the standard dispersal kernel, calculated on the mean number of rainy days, or from the extreme dispersal kernel, calculated from the maximum number of rainy days. The model would then move toads from colonised points to all possible points in the zone under the chosen kernel, and determine whether each possible point was colonised or not in the given wet season. Following this step, we added an additional (within time-step) step to the model -- the "control step". This control step determines whether toads that have colonised a potential point (either at this step or in a previous step) will survive the dry season. For natural waterpoints (springs and soaks) survival is determined by whether or not the point dries out in the given year (given by drying probabilities described above). If a natural point dries out in that year then survival is zero, else it is one.

For non-natural points, survival probability is given by the efficacy of that control option in that year. Control point efficacy is determined probabilistically for each waterpoint and depends upon the type of control action that has been performed at each point. For waterpoints that are tanks/troughs, we assume complete success or failure with a 1% failure rate. This is a lower probability than that assumed by Southwell but is justified here by the fact that these waterpoints are monitored at least fortnightly by pastoralists, and that the design of the TCZ involves an annual audit of all infrastructure early in the dry season with the intention that any failed infrastructure will be repaired early in the dry season. This infrastructure only needs to be effective for 5-10 days in the dry season for all toads at the point to die of dehydration.

For the control step, for natural waterpoints and for tank/troughs, we assume failure is complete, so for for this set of waterpoints we draw a failure outcome from a Bernoulli distribution given the failure probability, and multiply the colonisation status (1 = colonised) of each waterpoint by the resulting outcome. In this way, controlled sites that are colonised in the wet season have a high probability of being completely controlled in the following dry season, before the model's next time step.

Our other main control type is fencing. The intention of this control type is to prevent adult toads discovering points where water is available year round. Fenced areas present much larger targets for dispersing toads than single points. To calculate the potential number of colonists arriving at a fenced area, we follow Southwell et al. (2016) and express the detection radius around these points as the effective radius yielding a circle of the same area as the fenced area. Where the fenced area itself was not directly surveyed, we approximated it from the audited fence length alone, assuming a square enclosure: with total fence length (perimeter) $\ell$, the side length is $\ell/4$ and the enclosed area is $(\ell/4)^2$, from which the effective radius follows as above. This effectively inflates the number of colonists that will arrive at each fenced area. For fencing, we assume that failure will scale with the length of fenceline. We assume a 5% chance of failure per kilometre of fenceline and per gate. We also assume that, for a given fenceline, individual toads will only ever explore 1/4 of the total length (*i.e.*, one side of a square fenced area) in an attempt to access the waterpoint. This assumption rests on the strong tendency for invasion front toads to travel in straight lines; they are unlikely to systematically explore an entire perimeter. If we denote the number of km of fenceline plus the number of gates as $g$, then the probability of a toad breaching the fence is approximately $p_{b,i} =1-(1-0.05)^\frac{g}{4}$. To determine the number of colonists successfully colonising a fenced area then, we take the number colonising in the absence of the fence, and draw the realised number of colonists, $c^*_i$, from a Binomial distribution. That is, $c^*_i \sim \text{Binom}(p_{b,i}, c_i)$. We consider the point to have failed when $c_i \geq 2$. Rather than emitting colonists in the next time step, we assume instead that these failures will be detected in each annual toad audit, and will trigger an eradication response. This will incur an additional cost (see below on cost optimisation), and also a 5% chance of eradication failure calculated in the same way as for tanks/troughs. In the event of an eradication failure, these points will go on to emit $\lambda$ propagules in the next time step.

#### Cost optimisation

We look to design an intervention that is effective, but also does not waste resources. To this end we define two objective functions around performance. The first is a no-compromise objective: a zero probability of toads breaching the barrier. Any design that compromises this objective will be rejected. A second objective is to minimise the total number of points occupied by toads over the 50 year time horizon. This second objective aligns with the aspirations of Karajarri, to look after their country; to preserve the ecological and cultural values of the region for future generations.

We evaluate these two objectives within a cost-effectiveness analysis framework rather than a full benefit-cost analysis. Monetising the ecological and cultural benefits of halting the toad invasion is both methodologically difficult and, for the present purposes, unnecessary: the primary goal is to identify the least costly design that meets the hard constraint, and to characterise the conservation gain delivered per dollar spent. We do not discount costs or benefits over the 50-year horizon. Discounting on the basis of time preference alone is a questionable foundation for decisions involving long-term ecological harm, where a breach of the zone in year 40 is no less damaging to the landscape and its custodians than a breach in year 10. Our cost-effectiveness metric is therefore

$$CE = \frac{\text{toad point-years avoided}}{\text{total cost (\$)}}$$

where toad point-years avoided is the difference in total waterpoint occupancy by toads, summed across all waterpoints and all years of the simulation, between the no-intervention counterfactual and the proposed design. Total cost is the sum of all capital and recurrent expenditure associated with the design across the 50-year period. Higher values of $CE$ indicate greater conservation gain per dollar invested.

To identify the cost-effective design we use a backward greedy algorithm. We begin with the full implementation scenario, in which every audited artificial waterpoint inside the TCZ receives the intervention identified during the infrastructure audit. We then iteratively remove interventions, testing at each step whether a given removal violates the hard constraint. Candidate removals are evaluated in descending order of cost, so that the most expensive interventions are tested first. If the most expensive remaining intervention can be safely removed, it is removed and the algorithm proceeds to the next step; if not, the next most expensive candidate is tested, and so on. This ordering ensures that the algorithm preferentially eliminates high-cost interventions before low-cost ones, maximising cost savings in the early stages of the search and minimising the total number of simulation evaluations required. The algorithm terminates when no remaining intervention can be safely removed without violating the hard constraint, yielding the minimum-cost design consistent with the zero-breach objective.

The hard constraint is operationalised by simulation: a candidate design is considered to satisfy the constraint if it produces zero breaches across all simulation replicates run for that design. Because we evaluate a finite number of replicates, this test is inherently stochastic. A design with a true breach probability $p$ will pass the filter with probability $(1-p)^n$, where $n$ is the number of replicates per evaluation. We ran $n = 20$ replicates per candidate evaluation during the greedy search. Under the rule of three, a result of zero breaches in 20 replicates implies a 95% upper confidence bound on the true breach probability of approximately 15%; the filter therefore provides a practical screen for designs with high breach risk rather than a guarantee of near-zero risk. To guard against stopping the algorithm prematurely on a false negative, candidate interventions that trigger a breach at this screening stage are retained in the design without further testing. The final selected design was re-evaluated with $n = 100$ replicates as a confirmatory step, providing a more precise characterisation of its breach probability under the full simulation protocol.
